`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/ne555.md`:

`````markdown
# ne555 — NE555 timer (DIP-8) / NE555 Timer (DIP-8)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 8; types: power 1, ground 1, signal 6

## View
Shape `dip`, 8 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: the TI figure is captioned for the NE555 "D, P, PS, OR PW PACKAGE" and "(TOP VIEW)", and shows the notch on top, 1–4 down the left and 8–5 down the right. I rendered PDF page 3 to an image and looked at the figure.

## Sources
1. Texas Instruments, NA555, NE555, SA555, SE555 xx555 Precision Timers, SLFS022K (Sept. 1973, revised March 2026), section 4, figure and Table 4-1. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ne555.pdf — covers the NE555 in P (PDIP), read PDF page 3, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure and Table 4-1 agree on all 8 pins. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- Name uses `DIP-8`, the same in all 16 locales: it holds only a proper name and a package name, so there is nothing to translate.
- `RESET` is written without its overbar. TI's table does not use one for this pin; the function text says active low.
- All timer pins, `OUT` included, are `signal` as planned.
- The 4.5 V to 16 V range of pin 8 is TI's table description; the SE555's 18 V is left out because this item is the NE555.
- The 20-pin FK package of the SE555 (with NC pins) is left out.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/lm317.md`:

`````markdown
# lm317 — LM317 adjustable regulator (TO-220) / LM317 einstellbarer Spannungsregler (TO-220)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 3; types: power 2, signal 1

## View
Shape `to`, package `to220`: label side towards the viewer, leads pointing down, pins left to right `1`, `2`, `3`. Basis: TI's Figure 5-2 is captioned "KCS or KCT Package, 3-Pin TO-220 (Top View), Legacy Chip". It draws the package on its side, tab with hole on the left and leads to the right, with 3 INPUT at the top, 2 OUTPUT in the middle, 1 ADJUST at the bottom. Turning that drawing 90° clockwise, so that the leads point down, moves the top lead to the right: left to right 1 ADJUST, 2 OUTPUT, 3 INPUT. A top view of a TO-220 looks at the plastic side, not the metal back, which is the catalog schema's label side. I rendered PDF page 5 to an image and looked at it.

## Sources
1. Texas Instruments, LM317 3-Pin Adjustable Regulator, SLVS044Z (September 1997, revised April 2025), section 5, Figure 5-2 and table Pin Functions, Metal Can Packages. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf — covers TO-220 (KCS, KCT), read PDF page 5, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure 5-2 and the table agree: ADJUST 1, INPUT 3, OUTPUT 2 and TAB. This confirms the order given in the task. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- Names follow TI's table (`ADJUST`, `OUTPUT`, `INPUT`); `adj` is a tag.
- `OUTPUT` and `INPUT` are `power` by the catalog schema ("any supply rail, input or output"); `ADJUST` is `signal`.
- The tab: TI's table lists OUTPUT as "2, TAB" and the figure labels the tab OUTPUT. It goes in the item's notes and the function of pin 2. The advice to insulate the heat sink is my own conclusion from that connection, not a sentence of the datasheet.
- TI's TO-220 column is headed "Legacy Chip"; the datasheet lists no other TO-220 pinout, and the KCS and KCT packages are the ones it covers. Makers other than TI were not checked.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/l78xx.md`:

`````markdown
# l78xx — L78xx fixed regulators (TO-220) / L78xx Festspannungsregler (TO-220)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 3; types: power 2, ground 1

## View
Shape `to`, package `to220`: label side towards the viewer, leads pointing down, pins left to right `1`, `2`, `3`. Basis: ST's Figure 2 is captioned "Pin connections (top view)". For TO-220 it draws the package on its side, tab with hole on the left and leads to the right, with OUTPUT at the top, GROUND in the middle, INPUT at the bottom. Turning that drawing 90° clockwise, so that the leads point down, moves the top lead to the right: left to right INPUT, GROUND, OUTPUT. I rendered both revisions' pages to images and looked at them.

## Sources
1. STMicroelectronics, L78 Positive voltage regulator ICs, DocID2143 Rev 34 (November 2016), section 2, Figure 2. Read from a copy at https://protostack.com.au/download/l7805.pdf, page 4, accessed 2026-11-04. Covers TO-220.
2. STMicroelectronics, L78xx, L78xxC Positive voltage regulators, Rev 19 (March 2008), section 2, Figure 2. Read from a copy at https://static.rapidonline.com/pdf/47-3550.pdf, page 6, accessed 2026-11-04. Covers TO-220.

Not reachable: ST's own https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/l78.pdf timed out or reset from here in every attempt (curl over HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1, WebFetch), so the newest revision was not read. A search result names Rev 38 of February 2025; that excerpt does not count as read. Both copies above are ST's own PDFs, hosted by others.

## Cross-check
Both revisions give the same lead order for TO-220. It confirms the order in the task (in, ground, out).

One difference, the tab: Rev 34 prints `GND` next to the TO-220 tab, while Rev 19 prints no label on the TO-220 tab, only on D²PAK and DPAK. I use Rev 34, the newer one; Rev 19 does not contradict it. The tab connection therefore rests on one revision.

Neither revision numbers the TO-220 leads. Nothing UNVERIFIED about names or order.

## Choices
- Numbers `1`, `2`, `3` are positions from left to right in the front view, because ST names the leads without numbers. The notes say so.
- Names follow ST's figure: `INPUT`, `GROUND`, `OUTPUT`.
- Types: `INPUT` and `OUTPUT` are `power` by the catalog schema; `GROUND` is `ground`.
- The TO-220FP has the same lead order in both revisions, so the notes mention it. Its tab is not labelled in either figure, so the page says nothing about it.
- Left out: D²PAK, DPAK and the TO-3 of Rev 19. Other makers' 78xx parts were not checked, and the page names ST's series only.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/lm358.md`:

`````markdown
# lm358 — LM358 dual op-amp (DIP-8) / LM358 Doppel-OPV (DIP-8)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 8; types: power 2, signal 6

## View
Shape `dip`, 8 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: TI's Figure 4-1 is captioned for the 8-pin packages including PDIP (package P) and ends in "Top View". The figure marks pin 1 with a dot at the top left and runs 1–4 down the left and 8–5 down the right. I rendered PDF page 3 to an image and looked at it. The figure has a dot, not a notch; the drawing rule of the `dip` shape is the same.

## Sources
1. Texas Instruments, LM158, LM258, LM2904, LM358 Industry-Standard Dual Operational Amplifiers, SLOS068AB (June 1976, revised October 2024), section 4, Figure 4-1 and Table 4-1. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm358.pdf — covers LM358 in P (PDIP, 8), read PDF page 3, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure and Table 4-1 agree on all 8 pins. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- `V-` is typed `power`, not `ground`: TI calls it the negative (lowest) supply, or ground in single-supply use, and a split-supply circuit has a real negative rail there. The function text states both uses.
- Pin names use ASCII minus (`IN1-`, `V-`) where TI prints an en dash, so that a search with a keyboard minus finds them.
- The 20-pin FK package is left out.
`````

`````markdown
# lm324 — LM324 quad op-amp (DIP-14) / LM324 Vierfach-OPV (DIP-14)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 14; types: power 2, signal 12

## View
Shape `dip`, 14 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: TI's Figure 5-1 is captioned for the 14-pin packages including PDIP (package N) and "(Top View)". It marks pin 1 with a dot at the top left and runs 1–7 down the left and 14–8 down the right. I rendered PDF page 3 to an image and looked at it.

## Sources

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure and Table 5-1 agree on all 14 pins. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

- Pin names use ASCII minus (`1IN-`, `VCC-`) where TI prints an en dash.
- The item's notes point out that the supply pins sit in the middle of the package (4 and 11), a usual wiring slip.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/sn74hc595.md`:

`````markdown
# sn74hc595 — SN74HC595 shift register (DIP-16) / SN74HC595 Schieberegister (DIP-16)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 16; types: power 1, ground 1, signal 2, data 12

## View
Shape `dip`, 16 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: TI's section 5 figure is captioned "D, N, NS, J, DB, or PW Package", "16-Pin SOIC, PDIP, SO, CDIP, SSOP, or TSSOP" and "Top View". It shows the notch on top, 1–8 down the left, 16–9 down the right. I rendered PDF page 3 to an image and looked at it.

## Sources
1. Texas Instruments, SN54HC595, SN74HC595 8-Bit Shift Registers With 3-State Output Registers, SCLS041J (December 1982, revised October 2021), section 5, figure and Table 5-1; sections 1, 3 and 8.1 for behaviour and the 2 V to 6 V range. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc595.pdf — covers SN74HC595N, PDIP (16), read PDF page 3 and the text, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure and Table 5-1 agree on 15 pins.

Disagreement inside the datasheet: Table 5-1 has no 16-pin number for VCC. Its VCC row shows a dash in the SOIC/PDIP column and 20 in the LCCC column. The figure of the 16-pin packages shows VCC at pin 16. I chose pin 16: the figure is explicit, and 16 is the only number the table leaves unused. The table's dash looks like an editing error. The same table also gives RCLK and SRCLK the same LCCC number (14), which does not touch this item. I report the VCC gap in case a reader compares the table.

Nothing UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- `OE` and `SRCLR` carry an overbar at TI, which plain text cannot show. Names stay `OE` and `SRCLR`, so that a search finds them, and the function text says active low.
- Types as planned: SER, SRCLK, RCLK and all Q outputs `data`; OE and SRCLR `signal`.
- `QH'` keeps TI's apostrophe and is quoted in the YAML.
- The 20-pin FK package is left out.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/uln2003.md`:

`````markdown
# uln2003 — ULN2003A Darlington array (DIP-16) / ULN2003A Darlington-Array (DIP-16)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 16; types: power 1, ground 1, signal 14

## View
Shape `dip`, 16 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: TI's Figure 4-1 is captioned "D, N, NS, and PW Package 16-Pin SOIC, PDIP, SO, and TSSOP Top View". It shows the notch on top, 1–8 down the left, 16–9 down the right. I rendered PDF page 3 to an image and looked at it.

## Sources
1. Texas Instruments, ULN200x, ULQ200x High-Voltage, High-Current Darlington Transistor Arrays, SLRS027T (December 1976, revised March 2025), section 4 (Figure 4-1, Table 4-1), sections 7.3, 7.4 and 8.4 for the COM pin. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/uln2003a.pdf — covers ULN2003AN, PDIP (16), read PDF page 3 and those sections, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure and Table 4-1 agree on all 16 pins. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

The common-cathode pin: Table 4-1 describes pin 9 (COM) as the common cathode node of the flyback diodes, required for inductive loads. Section 7.4 says to tie it to the coil supply for inductive loads and allows it to float for resistive loads. Section 8.4 says it is typically tied to the system supply and warns against outputs far above the COM voltage. All of this is in the item's notes and the pin's notes, in my own words.

## Choices
- `COM` is typed `power`, though it does not supply the chip: section 8.4 says the device needs no supply of its own and COM typically goes to the system supply, and TI's table gives it no input or output direction. A reader who meets a red pin will connect it to a rail, which is the right wiring for coils. The notes say it may stay open for resistive loads.
- `E` is typed `ground`: TI says it is typically tied to ground.
- Inputs `nB` and outputs `nC` are `signal`.
- Item name is `ULN2003A`, the part the id stands for. The datasheet also covers ULN2002A, ULN2003AI, ULQ2003A, ULN2004A and ULQ2004A in the same figure; they are not named on the page.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/atmega328p.md`:

`````markdown
# atmega328p — ATmega328P microcontroller (DIP-28) / ATmega328P Mikrocontroller (DIP-28)

Kind: authoritative maker document
Pins: 28; types: power 2, ground 2, signal 2, io 22

## View
Shape `dip`, 28 pins: package from above, notch at the top, pin 1 top left, numbers counter-clockwise. Basis: Microchip's Figure 1-1 draws "28 SPDIP" with the notch on top, 1–14 down the left and 28–15 down the right. That one caption does not say "Top View", unlike the three other packages of the same figure (32 TQFP, 28 VQFN, 32 VQFN, all "Top View"). The notch on top with pin 1 at the top left and counter-clockwise numbers only fits a view from above, so I derive the view from that numbering rule. I rendered PDF page 12 to an image and looked at it.

## Sources
1. Microchip, ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P Data Sheet Complete, DS40002061B (Rev. B, 08/2020), Figure 1-1 (page 12), section 1.1 Pin Descriptions (pages 13–14), Alternate Functions of Ports B, C and D. https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/MCU08/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf — covers ATmega328P-PU in package 28P3, the 28-lead SPDIP, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
One maker document is enough here. Figure 1-1 and the port tables agree on every alternative function I list. No disagreement, nothing UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- Pin 1 is named `PC6/RESET`, the heading of section 1.1.5, and typed `signal`: with the RSTDISBL fuse unprogrammed it is the reset input. A pin note covers the fuse case. The port name is still in the name, as the task asks.
- GPIOs (PB, PC0–PC5, PD) are `io`. AVCC is `power`; AREF is `signal`.
- Function text lists every alternative function of the figure, with a short gloss in English and German. `SS` has an overbar in the figure; the text says active low.
- The two GND pins are 8 and 22, each its own table row.
- Left out: ADC6 and ADC7, which exist only in TQFP and VQFN (section 1.1.9), stated in the notes. The PB6/PB7 fuse note is short; the clock chapter holds the details.
- OC outputs are called "compare output", following the datasheet's "Output Compare Match". They are the PWM outputs, which the tag `pwm` covers.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/ics/to92.md`:

`````markdown
# to92 — TO-92 examples / TO-92: Beispiele

Kind: authoritative maker document (one per part)
Pins: 3 per variant, 7 variants; types: bc547, q2n2222, q2n3904, q2n7000: signal 3 each; lm35: power 1, signal 1, ground 1; reg78l05: power 2, ground 1; tl431: signal 2, ground 1

## View
Every variant is written for the same view, the shape `to`, package `to92`: flat side towards the viewer, leads pointing down, positions `1`, `2`, `3` from left to right.

How a datasheet's drawing maps to that view, which I rendered to images and looked at:

- **View from the lead end, flat side at the top of the drawing:** rotating the part about the left-right axis until the leads point down brings the flat side to the viewer and keeps left and right. Left to right stays as drawn.
- **View from the lead end, flat side at the bottom of the drawing:** left and right swap.
- **"Top view" lying on its side, flat side on the right, leads going away from the viewer:** the top item ends up on the right in the front view, the bottom item on the left.

Applied:

| Variant | What the source shows | Front view left to right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bc547 | onsemi case 29-11 end view: flat side at top, solid lead squares, "1" under the left lead; style 17 | 1 C, 2 B, 3 E |
| q2n2222 | Fairchild ZA03D drawing in the datasheet: end view flat side at top, "1 2 3" left to right; page 1 figure labelled "E B C" | 1 E, 2 B, 3 C |
| q2n3904 | same case 29-11 drawing; style 1 | 1 E, 2 B, 3 C |
| q2n7000 | onsemi case 135AN: end view flat side at top, "1 2 3" left to right; "1 – Source, 2 – Gate, 3 – Drain" | 1 S, 2 G, 3 D |
| lm35 | TI "LP Package, 3-Pin TO-92 (Bottom View)": flat side at top, +VS VOUT GND over 1 2 3 | 1 +VS, 2 VOUT, 3 GND |
| reg78l05 | TI Figure 5-2 "LP Package, 3-Pin TO-92 (Top View)": flat side right, INPUT, COMMON, OUTPUT from top to bottom | 1 OUTPUT, 2 COMMON, 3 INPUT |
| tl431 | TI "LP (TO-92/TO-226) PACKAGE (TOP VIEW)": flat side right, CATHODE, ANODE, REF from top to bottom | 1 REF, 2 ANODE, 3 CATHODE |

TI's generic TO-92 outline LP0003A agrees with this reading: its end view has the flat side at the bottom and "3 2 1" from left to right, which is 1, 2, 3 in the front view.

## Position numbers against datasheet numbers
The numbers in this item are always positions in the front view, as the task asks. They equal the maker's own numbers except in one case:

- **TL431, TI:** Table 5-1 gives LP as CATHODE 1, ANODE 2, REF 3. So TI's pin 1 (CATHODE) is at position 3 and TI's pin 3 (REF) is at position 1. This is stated in the pin notes of the variant. onsemi's TL431/D numbers the same leads 1 Reference, 2 Anode, 3 Cathode, equal to the positions.

TI's own material is not consistent here: the LP0003A outline puts pin 1 on the left in the front view, while the TL431 table and top-view figure put number 1 (CATHODE) on the right. I follow the figure with its names, since it states where each named lead is, and because onsemi's independent document gives the same physical order (reference on the left, cathode on the right).

## Sources
1. onsemi, Amplifier Transistors BC546B, BC547A, B, C, BC548B, C, BC546/D Rev. 8 (August 2021), page 1 and case outline 29-11 with style list, PDF pages 6–7. https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/bc546-d.pdf — bc547, accessed 2026-11-04.
2. onsemi (Fairchild), PN2222A NPN General-Purpose Amplifier, Rev. 1.1.0 (July 2014), datasheet pages 1 and 4 (PDF pages 2 and 5). https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/pn2222a-d.pdf — q2n2222, accessed 2026-11-04. **This datasheet covers the plastic PN2222A in TO-92, not a 2N2222.**
3. onsemi, P2N2222A Amplifier Transistors, P2N2222A/D Rev. 7 (January 2013), page 1 (case 29, style 17: 1 collector, 2 base, 3 emitter). https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/p2n2222a-d.pdf — only for the warning in the notes, accessed 2026-11-04.
4. multicomp, 2N2222 Low Power Bipolar Transistors, sheet V1.0 of 06/04/06, page 1 (TO-18 metal can, leads in a triangle). Read from a copy at https://wp.kntu.ac.ir/shamsi/Electronic1/Datasheet/BJT/2N2222.pdf — only for the warning in the notes, accessed 2026-11-04.
5. onsemi, General Purpose Transistors 2N3903, 2N3904, 2N3903/D Rev. 9 (August 2021), page 1 and case outline, PDF pages 7–8. https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/2n3903-d.pdf — q2n3904, accessed 2026-11-04.
6. onsemi, N-Channel Enhancement Mode Field Effect Transistor 2N7000, 2N7002, NDS7002A, NDS7002A/D Rev. 11 (March 2025), page 1 and case 135AN outline, PDF page 8. https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/nds7002a-d.pdf — q2n7000, accessed 2026-11-04.
7. Texas Instruments, LM35 Precision Centigrade Temperature Sensors, SNIS159H (August 1999, revised December 2017), section 5, page 3. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm35.pdf — lm35, accessed 2026-11-04.
8. Texas Instruments, UA78L, SLVS010X (January 1976, revised June 2023), section 5, Figure 5-2 and pin table, page 3; covers the UA78L05 in LP. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ua78l.pdf — reg78l05, accessed 2026-11-04.
9. onsemi, MC78L00A Series, NCV78L00A Positive Voltage Regulators, MC78L00A/D Rev. 21 (July 2025), page 1 (1 Output, 2 Ground, 3 Input) and case 29-10 outline, PDF page 14. https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/mc78l00a-d.pdf — reg78l05 cross-check, accessed 2026-11-04.
10. Texas Instruments, TL431, TL432, SLVS543S (August 2004, revised May 2024), section 5, LP figure and Table 5-1, page 4; LP0003A outline, PDF page 72. https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tl431.pdf — tl431, accessed 2026-11-04.
11. onsemi, TL431A, B Series Programmable Precision References, TL431/D Rev. 45 (November 2025), page 1 (1 Reference, 2 Anode, 3 Cathode). https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/tl431-d.pdf — tl431 cross-check, accessed 2026-11-04.

## Cross-check
- One maker document is enough per part; 78L05 and TL431 also have a second maker, and both agree on the physical order.
- bc547: onsemi prints "OBSOLETE" across page 1 of the BC546/D sheet, a notice about onsemi's own production. The pinout is still what that sheet states; it was not checked against other makers.
- q2n7000: the same onsemi sheet numbers the SOT-23 2N7002 differently (1 Gate, 2 Source, 3 Drain). Only the TO-92 row is used.
- Case outlines: BC546/D and 2N3903/D use case 29-11, NDS7002A/D uses 135AN, MC78L00A/D uses 29-10, PN2222A uses Fairchild's ZA03D. All have pin 1 on the left in the front view.
- A web search summary reported a "conflict" for the 2N7000; reading the sheet shows it was the SOT-23 row. No real conflict.
- Nothing UNVERIFIED and no GEOMETRY UNVERIFIED.

## Choices
- **q2n2222 is the PN2222A.** The variant's name says `PN2222A`, the id stays `q2n2222`, and `2n2222` is a tag so that a search finds it. The item's notes and the note on pin 1 say it does not apply to the metal-can 2N2222, whose TO-18 can has its leads in a triangle, or to the P2N2222A, which runs the other way round (collector left). I chose the PN2222A because a maker's datasheet for it exists; a true "2N2222A in TO-92" is not in the sources I read.
- Transistor leads are `signal`: none of them is a supply by nature. The short names `C`, `B`, `E`, `S`, `G`, `D` stay language-neutral, and the words are in the function.
- `ANODE` of the TL431 is `ground`: TI calls it the common pin, normally connected to ground. The TL431 can also serve in negative references, which the type colour does not show. `CATHODE` and `REF` are `signal`.
- `COMMON` of the 78L05 follows TI's name; onsemi says Ground. The notes point out that the 78L05 runs opposite to the L78xx in TO-220, which follows from comparing the two items.
- LM35: `+VS` follows TI; the sheet's other packages (TO-CAN, SOIC, TO-220) have other numbers and are left out.
- Variant order follows the task.
`````

`documentation/ecalc-sources/pinouts/SUMMARY.md`:

`````markdown
# pinouts — summary

47 items in six groups. No item was left out, and no pin number or name is unverified. Each file names which view its drawing is
written for and on what that rests.

| Folder | Items | Main sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data/` | 11 | USB-IF specifications (USB 2.0, USB 3.x, Type-C 2.5); makers and cable vendors for HDMI, DisplayPort, VGA, RJ45 and RS-232, whose standards were not read |
| `audio/` | 4 | Neutrik, Amphenol and ITT Cannon drawings for XLR; the MIDI Association for MIDI; maker documents for the jacks |
| `pc_power/` | 9 | PCI Express CEM figures, Intel's 4-wire fan specification, PSU and board makers |
| `boards/` | 6 | Arduino, Espressif, the NodeMCU project and Raspberry Pi documents, including their figures |
| `debug/` | 8 | ARM, SEGGER, Microchip, FTDI, SparkFun, Adafruit and Seeed documents; several independent sources for OBD-II and hobby servos |
| `ics/` | 9 | The makers' datasheets for the package drawn |

## Weakest points

- **Standards not read:** HDMI, VESA DisplayPort, TIA-232, TIA-568, IEEE 802.3, SAE J1962, ISO 15031-3 and AES14 are paywalled. The items rest on independent
  reproductions, as each file says.
- **`displayport`:** the view is implied: it rests on device-port pictures plus one caption, and no maker drawing could be opened. The sink side's CONFIG ground rule is left out.
- **`usb_micro_b`:** the receptacle is the mirror image of the labelled plug figure.
- **`rj45`:** pictures only, no text states the view; four documents agree.
- **`hdmi_a`:** the HEAC polarity of pins 14 and 19 differs between sources (+ on 14 chosen). The +5 V current is 50 or 55 mA, and the notes state both.
- **PoE polarity:** sources conflict, so the item states only which pins form each pole.
- **`molex_4`:** one Maxtor drawing plus the mirror rule; the side of the cut corners is the least certain detail.
- **`sata_data`, `sata_power`:** the direction of the L step rests on one Intel figure, one Gigabyte drawing and the SATA-IO row order.
- **`eps_8`, `fan_3`:** the view is derived from the connector family.
- **`xlr`:** the drawn key is the latch. AES14 itself was not read; pin functions rest on Rane, Shure and Mackie, geometry on the makers' drawings.
- **`qwiic`:** both makers' schematics say pin 1 = GND, but SparkFun's cable drawing says pin 1 = SCL. GND was chosen, and a note warns. JST's catalogue could not be read, so
  `qwiic` and `grove` state the sequence of the pins, not which physical end is pin 1.
- **`servo`:** the wire colours rest on a few makers, and the numbers `S`, `+`, `-` are used because Parallax and SparkFun number in opposite directions.
- **`arm_jtag_20`, `arm_swd_10`, `avr_isp_6`:** the side of the key comes from drawings; Arm's overview says it is no specification. SEGGER differs on JTAG pins 14 to 20 (5 V output on 19, in the notes).
- **`esp8266_nodemcu`:** a text file in the project's repository swaps D1 and D2 against the schematic, the pin map and the firmware documents; those three were followed. Clones differ. No ESP-12E datasheet was read.
- **`raspberry_pi_40`:** SPI1 and PWM on GPIO18 to GPIO21 were checked only against the BCM2711.
- **`l78xx`:** st.com could not be reached; ST's PDFs were read on third-party hosts (rev 34 of 2016 and rev 19 of 2008). The lead order agrees in both.
- **`bc547`:** onsemi's sheet is marked obsolete, and no other maker was checked.
- **`to92`:** TI's table and its generic outline disagree on the TL431's pin numbers; the named figure and onsemi agree, so positions are used and the notes give TI's numbers.

## Judgement calls on types

Read these before relying on the colours: `V-` and `VCC-` of the op-amps and `COM` of the ULN2003A are `power`, `ANODE` of the TL431 is `ground`. The flash lines of the ESP32
(GPIO6 to GPIO11) and the NodeMCU are `data`, not `io`, so they do not look like free pins. GPIO0 and GPIO1 of the Raspberry Pi are `nc` (reserved for the HAT EEPROM, marked
"do not connect"). Manufacturer pins of OBD-II are `nc` although they can be live, which the function text says.
`````

````text
- Query API of tables and codes: `SearchAll` ranks the three kinds together (equal ranks keep calculators, then tables, then codes) and `Overview` leaves out categories without items. The id of an item of another kind answers `not_a_calculator`, `not_a_table` or `not_a_code`. `QueryTable` formats the cells in the column units (a column with an empty `unit` writes each number with its own prefix): a cell of a generated table with 4 significant digits, a cell of a transcribed table (no `generate`) with up to 9 (`transcribedSig`; the shortest decimal prints, so a published number is never shortened: 434.79 MHz, 2.4835 GHz, never 434.8 MHz), a result computed by `interp` always with 4. It adds the SI numbers rounded to 12 significant digits, limits `filter` to `MaxFilterLength` (128) characters, an item `id` (and the `kind` of decode and encode) to `MaxIDLength` (256) characters (a longer one is the unknown-id error at the top of `lookup`, `lookupTable`, `lookupCodeItem` and `ResolveItem`, before the search for close matches, and is not echoed) and the page to `MaxTableLimit` (50) rows, and answers a lookup that finds nothing with `found: false`, not with an error. `ge` is the row with the smallest cell that is still at least the value (equal cells: the first in table order), which is the first qualifying row on a column that rises and the smallest fit on a falling one such as the AWG diameters (AWG 18 for 1 mm, not 4/0); it differs from the expression function `lookup_ge`, which stays the first row in table order because the finders rely on it. `interp` needs a strictly monotonic x column. `QueryDecode`/`QueryEncode` accept a code kind or the id of a code item, keep the code of a `CodeError` and leave NaN values and empty lists out of the JSON (an embedded `CodeResult` would bring its `MarshalJSON` along).
````

````text
- Pinout items: `Load` reads `pinouts/*.yaml` after the codes (kind `pinout`, category `pinouts`, `group` one of `data audio pc_power boards debug ics`). A pin has `number` (1 to 8 characters, unique), `name` (1 to 24, language neutral), `function` (English and German), `type` (`power ground signal data io nc`), optional `wire` (an id of `pinstyles.yaml`, only when a source names the colour) and optional `notes`. An item has `pins` or at least two `variants` with the same pin numbers, never both. The `shape` is one of `rows dip to circular jack board`; every pin is drawn exactly once, every position names a pin, unused shape fields are refused, and `views` (plug and socket captions) exist exactly when the shape is drawn as plug or socket. Adding a shape field or an outline is a change to the loader, the catalog JSON, `ecalc-pinout-draw.js` and its tests together.
- Pin styles: `catalog/pinstyles.yaml` is data, not theme: a pin type reads the same on every skin. The six types and fifteen wire ids are fixed and in this order, every ink has a WCAG contrast of at least 4.5 on its fill (checked at load), names exist in all 16 locales. Without `pinstyles.yaml` a catalog without pinouts still loads (empty `pin_types` and `wires`); with pinouts the file is required.
- Pinout JSON: the top level carries `pin_types` and `wires`; a pinout item always has all 14 keys and its `shape` all 16 keys (`""`, `null` or `[]` when the type does not use one); `views` is `null` for shapes with one fixed view, a gap in a board or row is `null`, `pins` of a shape is a number for a dip and a list for a `to`.
- Pinout vectors: every pinout has `testdata/vectors/pinouts/<id>.json` and every file an item; per variant the `counts` of all six types are exact (their sum is the pin count) and at least three pins (all when fewer) are checked by number, name and type, each with its source in `ref`.
- Query API of pinouts: `SearchAll` ranks the pinouts as the fourth kind (equal ranks keep calculators, tables, codes, pinouts), `ItemCount` and `Overview` count them, and the id of a pinout answers `not_a_calculator`, `not_a_table` or `not_a_code` where another kind was asked for (`not_a_pinout` the other way round). `QueryPinout` reads the pins of one variant in English: `pin` equals a number or a name exactly and case-insensitively (several pins can share a name, all are returned), a `pin` that matches nothing is `found: false` with the `variants`, not an error; an unknown `variant` is `unknown_variant` and lists the ids; `filter` (at most `MaxFilterLength`) matches number, name, function and notes in English and German; the page is 1 to `MaxPinoutLimit` (50) pins. `connector` and `view` are derived from the shape (`pinoutConnector`, `pinoutView`; every outline of `PinoutOutlines` needs an English name in `pinoutOutlineNames`), `wire` is the English colour name. `DescribePinout` lists group, connector, view, pin count, variants, pins per type, notes and source and no pins. The tests of these functions use fixture pinouts, and the bound test also loops over the shipped ones.
- Pinout content: `catalog/pinouts/<group>.yaml` holds what people wire from, so a wrong pin can destroy a board. Pin numbers, names and the drawing direction come from what was read: a maker's document or a free official specification for its own part, two independent sources otherwise, and an unverified detail stays out. `rows`, `positions` and the board lists are written in the view the item states; the other view is the mirror image, never a second list. The outlines are fixed in that view, and the data was written against them: `rj45` latch notch at the bottom, `displayport` cut corner at the lower left, `hdmi_a`, `usb_mini_b`, `usb_micro_b`, `dsub` and `obd2` wide side up, `usb_b` chamfers on top, `usb_a` tongue of the receptacle in the upper half, `minifit` latch on top, `molex` cut corners at the bottom, `sata_data` and `sata_power` L step at the bottom next to S7 and P1.
````

`````markdown
# Chapter 32: ECalc – electronics formulas in the Virtual Desktop

ECalc is a formula collection for electronics in the Virtual Desktop. A calculator page shows the circuit, the formula and the results side by side, and it recalculates while you type. You enter the values you know and ECalc works out the rest. For resistors it also suggests the nearest standard value from an E series, and the standard-value combiner finds standard values that reach a target resistance, in series or in parallel.

ECalc has 79 calculators in ten categories, 44 reference tables (see [Tables](#tables)), five component code pages (see [Component Codes](#component-codes)) and 47 pinouts of connectors, board headers and ICs (see [Pinouts](#pinouts)). The agent can calculate with the same formulas, read the tables, codes and pinouts, and open a calculator for you (see [Using ECalc from the Agent](#using-ecalc-from-the-agent)). ECalc runs in your browser. It needs no provider and has no switch of its own in **Config**.

## Table of Contents
1. [Opening ECalc](#opening-ecalc)
2. [Finding a Calculator](#finding-a-calculator)
3. [The Calculator Page](#the-calculator-page)
4. [Entering Values](#entering-values)
5. [Standard Values (E Series)](#standard-values-e-series)
6. [Settings](#settings)
7. [The Calculators](#the-calculators)
8. [Tables](#tables)
9. [Component Codes](#component-codes)
10. [Pinouts](#pinouts)
11. [Sources and Honesty](#sources-and-honesty)
12. [Using ECalc from the Agent](#using-ecalc-from-the-agent)
13. [Privacy and Safety](#privacy-and-safety)
14. [When Something Goes Wrong](#when-something-goes-wrong)

---

## Opening ECalc

Open **ECalc** from the start menu, in the category **Development**. The window opens at about 1100 × 760 pixels and you can
resize it. ECalc reopens on the calculator you used last.

The window has three columns: a **category rail** on the left, a **list** of calculators in the middle and the **calculator
page** on the right. In a narrow window (below about 720 pixels) the three become one stack. Choose a category, then a
calculator, and use **Back** to return to the previous level.

## Finding a Calculator

- **Category rail:** **Favorites** and **Recent** come first, followed by the categories that hold items: Basics, Passive,
  Filters, Semiconductors, Power supply, Op-amps, Timers, RF, Digital, Wiring & PCB, **Tables**, **Codes** and **Pinouts**. Each
  category shows how many items it holds. The rail lists a category only when it has content.
- **Search:** type in the search box at the top to find a calculator, a table, a component code or a pinout by its name in your language, by
  its English name or by a keyword such as "divider". Each item has keywords, and the search matches them too.
- **Favorites:** the favorite button on a calculator page adds it to **Favorites**. Click it again to remove it.
- **Recent:** ECalc remembers the last 12 calculators you opened.

## The Calculator Page

A calculator page has these parts:

- **Title bar:** the name of the calculator and the buttons **Add to favorites**, **Copy results** and **Reset to defaults**.
- **Schematic:** the circuit, with an input field next to each component it belongs to. A calculator without a schematic shows
  its fields in a plain list.
- **Formula:** the formula in typeset form, and below it a live line with your values filled in, for example
  *V_out = 12 V · 2.2 kΩ / (4.7 kΩ + 2.2 kΩ) = 3.83 V*.
- **Nearest standard values:** the E-series suggestions for the resistors (see [Standard Values (E Series)](#standard-values-e-series)).
- **Combinations:** only on the **Standard-value combiner**. It shows the nearest single standard value to the target, and up to
  five pairs in series and up to five pairs in parallel, each with its value and its deviation from the target. The block is
  headed with the series you chose, for example "Combinations of E24 values".
- **Derived values:** further quantities that follow from the result, for example the current through a divider and its power.
- **Chart:** a curve under the formula. It plots one value against another from 0 to an end value, and every other value stays at
  the value on the page. The RC time constant, for example, draws the capacitor voltage over time from 0 to 5 τ. The chart stays
  hidden while the values it needs are unknown.
- **Warnings:** a note when the values do not make sense, for example an output voltage that is not below the input voltage.
- **Explanation:** a collapsible text about the calculator, with its **Source**: the standard, datasheet or textbook behind the
  formula.

**Copy results** puts the values of the page on the clipboard. **Reset to defaults** restores the starting values of the
calculator.

**Dimmed fields:** some calculators offer an option, such as the power system of a cable (DC, single-phase AC or three-phase
AC). A field that the selected option does not use is dimmed, and its tooltip reads "Not used with the selected option". For
DC in the **Cable voltage drop** calculator, for example, cos φ is dimmed. Dimmed fields are left out of **Copy results** and of
the E-series suggestions.

## Entering Values

Every calculator needs a fixed number of known values. Ohm's law, for example, needs two of the four quantities voltage,
current, resistance and power. The fields you fill in are **inputs**. ECalc fills the other fields with **computed** values and
tints them.

- **Change what is known:** type into a computed field. It becomes an input, and the input you edited longest ago becomes
  computed. This way you can work from whichever value you have at hand.
- **Lock a value:** the lock icon on a field pins it. A locked field stays an input until you unlock it, even when you edit
  other fields.
- **Number formats:** you can type `4k7` (4.7 kΩ), `2u2` (2.2 µ), `10 mA`, `1e-6` or `0,5`. A decimal comma and a decimal point
  both work. A unit after the number is optional.
- **Number systems:** the four fields of the **Number systems** calculator (dec, hex, bin, oct) show the same whole number, each in
  its own base. Type the number into any of them, using the digits of that field's base. The prefix of that base is optional: `0x`
  for hexadecimal (`0xFF`), `0b` for binary (`0b1111_1111`) and `0o` for octal (`0o377`). Decimal takes plain digits (`255`), and
  `_` or a space may separate the digits. Long hexadecimal and binary results are grouped for readability, by four digits in
  hexadecimal (`0xDEAD_BEEF`) and by eight in binary (`0b1_00000000`).
- **Units:** the dropdown next to a field chooses the unit, and it offers only the units that suit the field. **Auto** picks a
  suitable prefix, such as mA or kΩ. A cross-section offers mm², AWG and kcmil, a temperature offers °C, °F and K, and the copper
  thickness of a PCB trace offers oz (copper weight). Some fields offer special units, such as dBm, dBV and dBu for levels, or
  mAh, Ah and Wh for charge and energy.
- **Lists:** the series and parallel calculator takes a list such as `4k7, 10k, 2k2`. Separate the entries with commas,
  semicolons or spaces. A comma directly in front of a digit is a decimal comma, so `4,7k, 10k` is two entries (4.7 kΩ and
  10 kΩ) while `1,2,3` is one entry that cannot be read; put a space after a comma that separates entries.
- **Display:** the results show a decimal comma in German, Czech, Danish, Greek, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Norwegian,
  Polish, Portuguese and Swedish, and a decimal point in the other languages. Lists always show a decimal point, because the
  comma separates their entries.

When something is wrong, the field shows a message instead of a number:

| Message | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| "Enter more values to calculate this." | The known values do not determine this field yet. |
| "These values give no finite result." | The calculation divides by zero or leaves the range of numbers. |
| "This value must be greater than zero." | Resistance, for example, cannot be zero or negative. |
| "Could not read this value. Examples: 4k7, 10 mA, 1e-6." | The text is not a number with an optional prefix and unit. Your previous values stay as they were. |

## Standard Values (E Series)

Resistors come in standard values. Every resistor field of a calculator shows **Nearest E24 value**: the closest standard
value and how far it is from the calculated one, in percent. For example, 4.7 kΩ is in the E24 series, and a calculated 4.6 kΩ
would show 4.7 kΩ with a deviation of about +2.2 %.

Choose another series (E6 to E192) in the **E series** selector. The default is E24. Series with more values, such as E96, give
a smaller deviation. ECalc remembers your choice.

**Standard-value combiner.** The calculator **Standard-value combiner** in the Basics category turns a target resistance into
standard values. It uses the same **E series** selector. It shows the nearest single value of the chosen series, and up to five
pairs in series and up to five pairs in parallel. Each pair shows its combined value and its deviation from the target in
percent. For example, 5 kΩ from E12 gives 4.7 kΩ + 270 Ω (−0.6 %), or 10 kΩ in parallel with 10 kΩ (exactly 5 kΩ).

## Settings

The settings menu has two options:

- **Significant digits:** how many digits the results show, from 3 to 6. The default is 4.
- **Schematic symbols:** **IEC** draws the resistor as a rectangle (the default). **ANSI** draws the zigzag resistor.

ECalc keeps its settings, your favorites, the recent list, the units you chose and the last values of each calculator in the
browser, under the key `aurago.ecalc.v1`. They stay in that browser. Nothing is stored on the AuraGo server, and clearing the
browser data resets them. ECalc works without browser storage too, it just forgets everything when you close the window.

## The Calculators

ECalc has 79 calculators in ten categories. Each table lists the calculators of one category, in the order of the category rail.
The source behind each formula, the standard, datasheet or textbook, is shown on the calculator's page under **Explanation**, so
the tables leave it out.

### Basics

| Calculator | What it does |
|------------|--------------|
| Ohm's law and power | Voltage, current, resistance and power. Enter any two and get the other two. |
| Voltage divider | The output voltage of a divider of two resistors. It also finds a resistor or the input voltage for a target output, and shows current and power. |
| Loaded voltage divider | The same divider with a load resistor on the output. It shows the unloaded output for comparison and warns when the load makes the target impossible. |
| Current divider | How a current splits between two parallel resistors. |
| Series and parallel resistors | The total resistance of a list of resistors, in series and in parallel. |
| Decibel ratio | Converts between a ratio and decibels. Choose voltage (20 log) or power (10 log). |
| dB levels | Voltage, resistance and power with the levels in dBm, dBV and dBu. |
| Wheatstone bridge | The bridge voltage from the supply and four resistors, or the resistor that balances the bridge. |
| Star-delta transform | Converts three delta resistors to the equivalent star, and back. |
| RMS, peak and average | Converts between the RMS, peak, peak-to-peak and average value of a sine, square or triangle wave. |
| Charge and energy | Converts between charge (for example the mAh of a battery), voltage and energy (Wh or J). |
| Standard-value combiner | The nearest single standard value to a target resistance, and series or parallel pairs that come closest. |

| Calculator | What it does |
|------------|--------------|

| Inductive reactance | Reactance of a coil. Any two of frequency, inductance and reactance give the third. |
| Series impedance (RC, RL, RLC) | Net reactance, impedance and phase of a resistor in series with a coil, a capacitor or both. |
| Parallel impedance (RC, RL, RLC) | Impedance, phase and equivalent parallel reactance of a resistor in parallel with a coil, a capacitor or both. |
| RC time constant | Charging and discharging of a capacitor through a resistor, with the time constant and the voltage curve. |
| Series and parallel capacitors | Total capacitance of a list of capacitors, in series and in parallel. |
| Series and parallel inductors | Total inductance of a list of coils, in series and in parallel, without mutual coupling. |
| Capacitor energy and charge | Energy, charge, voltage and capacitance of a capacitor. Any two of them give the other two. |
| Air-core coil (Wheeler) | Inductance of a single-layer air-core coil from its diameter, length and turns, or any one of them for a wanted inductance. |
| Toroid inductance (A_L) | Inductance of a toroid core from its A_L value and the number of turns, or any one of the three. |
| Wire resistance | DC resistance of a copper, aluminium or silver conductor, with temperature correction. Also solves for the length, cross-section or temperature. |

## Tables

The **Tables** category holds 44 reference tables. 40 are transcribed from standards and published sources. The other 4 are generated by ECalc from formulas: the AWG wire gauges, the PCB trace width after IPC-2221 and the two E-series tables. Open a table from the category. The list is sorted into the groups **Conductors and Cables**, **Components**, **Materials** and **General**.

On the table page:

- **Filter:** type in the filter box, or press `/` to jump to it. The filter keeps the rows in which a shown cell contains the text.
- **Sort:** click a column header to sort the rows ascending or descending, or back in table order. Empty cells always come last.
- **Units:** each column has its own unit dropdown, with the units that suit it (a cross-section can be shown as mm², kcmil or AWG). ECalc remembers your choice for that column of that table.
- **Digits:** the numbers of a table transcribed from a standard are shown with every digit they were written with (434.79 MHz, 2.4835 GHz), whatever the significant-digit setting says; the setting applies to the computed tables (AWG, IPC-2221 widths, E24 and E192) and to a value you convert into another unit.
- **Empty columns:** a column without any value is hidden. The line under the table says how many columns are hidden: "Columns without verified data are hidden: N".
- **Copy table:** copies the visible rows, in the units shown, as tab-separated text that you can paste into a spreadsheet.
- **Banners and notes:** a table marked as guide values shows a banner: the values are guide values from the cited source, and the standard itself is authoritative. A table with mains installation data shows a mains note: the applicable national rules decide, and the installation work is for qualified persons. Each table names its source and shows its notes.
- **Finders:** two calculators select a row of a table, the **Cable cross-section finder** and the **PCB conductor spacing finder (IPC-2221)**. Their card sits on the table page, shows the inputs that are still free and hides the fixed choice of the finder. The row that matches the result is highlighted and scrolled into view, and the highlight moves when you change the inputs. If the inputs lie outside the verified data, the finder shows the warning "Not covered by the verified data" and highlights no row.

## Component Codes

The **Codes** category decodes component markings and writes them from a value. There is one page for each kind of code:

- **Resistor colour code** and **Inductor colour code**: the colour bands. Click a band to choose its colour in the menu, or use the keyboard: Tab moves to a band, Enter, Space or the down arrow opens its menu, the arrow keys move through the colours, Enter picks one and Escape closes the menu. The page shows the value, the tolerance and, for six-band resistors, the temperature coefficient, and it gives the nearest standard value of the chosen series. Inductors have four or five bands.
- **SMD resistor codes**: the three-digit code (472 is 4.7 kΩ), the four-digit code, the EIA-96 code (01C) and the R notation (4R7 is 4.7 Ω). A value that you enter shows its three-digit, four-digit and EIA-96 marking.
- **Capacitor codes**: the picofarad code (104 is 100 nF, 4p7 is 4.7 pF), the tolerance letter and the voltage code. A marking can have up to three parts, for example `104K 1H`: 100 nF, ±10 % and 50 V.
- **Ceramic capacitor temperature codes**: class 1 (temperature compensating, for example C0G or NP0) with its temperature coefficient in ppm/K and its tolerance, and class 2 (high permittivity, for example X7R or U2J) with its temperature range and the permitted capacitance change. A class 2 code has no value of its own, so the page shows no number for it.

Resistor colours follow IEC 60062:2016. Where makers still print an older tolerance reading, the page shows it as a warning. Voltage codes are a maker convention, so the page says so and the datasheet decides. Warnings and error messages come from the engine and are in English in every language.

## Pinouts

The **Pinouts** category holds 47 pinouts of connectors, board headers, IC packages and other parts with pins. Open a pinout from the category. The list is sorted into the groups **Data and video**, **Audio**, **PC power and fans**, **Boards**, **Debug and interfaces** and **ICs**; the groups are listed at the end of this section.

A pinout page shows:

- **The drawing:** ECalc draws the part from its shape and its pin list. It is a drawing, not a photo.
- **The title bar:** the name, the favorite button and **Copy pinout**.
- **Variant:** a choice of variants, on the pinouts that have them.
- **View:** a choice of plug or socket, on the pinouts that have two views. The caption next to it reads **Looking at the mating face**.
- **Pin types:** a legend of the pin types that the pinout uses.
- **Detail panel:** the function, type, wire and notes of the selected pin.
- **Pin table:** the columns **Pin**, **Name**, **Function**, **Type**, **Wire** and **Notes**. The Wire column appears only when a pin of the variant has a wire colour.
- **Notes and source:** the notes of the pinout and the source it was taken from, at the foot of the page.

**Two views.** 31 of the 47 pinouts have a **View** choice. Their two views carry the names of the item, for example *Plug (cable end)* and *Receptacle (on the host or hub)*. The drawing shows the contacts as you see them when you look at the mating face, the face that meets the other part. A plug and its socket face each other when they are mated, so seen from their mating faces they are mirror images: left and right swap. ECalc draws the view that the pinout stores as its drawn view as it is, and the other view as the mirror image. Numbers and names stay readable, but the contacts move to the other side of the drawing. Boards and ICs have one fixed view and no choice. The Raspberry Pi 40-pin header is the one board with a View choice.

**Pin colours.** Each contact is filled with the colour of its pin type. The legend names the types the pinout uses:

| Type | Colour | What it means |
|------|--------|---------------|
| Power | red | A supply voltage, such as VBUS or +5 V |
| Ground | dark slate | The return or earth connection, GND |
| Signal | amber | A control, status or analogue line, such as an audio channel, a reset or the speed signal of a fan |
| Data | blue | A line of a data link, such as the USB D+ and D- lines |
| General-purpose I/O | green | A pin that the user programs, such as a GPIO pin of a board |
| Not connected | grey | A pin that is not connected or reserved, or a key position without a pin |

**Wire colours.** A wire colour is shown only where a standard or guide names one, for example for USB Type-A, RJ45, ATX, FTDI, Qwiic, Grove and the servo cable. Some cables differ from those colours. The ATX notes say to go by position, not by colour.

**Variants.** Four pinouts have variants. RJ45 (8P8C) has T568A and T568B, which differ only in the wire colours of the green and orange pairs. The 3.5 mm headset jack (TRRS) has CTIA (AHJ) and OMTP. DisplayPort has the Source side (output) and the Sink side (monitor input), which number pins 1 to 12 differently. TO-92: examples has seven part examples: BC547, PN2222A, 2N3904, 2N7000, LM35, 78L05 and TL431.

**Hover, click and filter.** Hovering a contact in the drawing or a row in the table highlights both. A click selects the pin: its details appear in the detail panel and its row is scrolled into view. A second click clears the selection. The drawing reacts to the pointer only; with the keyboard, use the pin number button at the start of each row. The filter box above the table matches the pin number, name, function, type name, wire colour name and notes. Pins that do not match are dimmed in the drawing and their rows are hidden. Press `/` to jump to the filter box, and Escape to clear it.

**Copy pinout** copies the rows that are shown, after the filter, for the chosen variant. The text is tab-separated and starts with a header line, so you can paste it into a spreadsheet. ECalc remembers the variant and the view of each pinout in the browser, with its other settings.

**Check the view before you wire anything.** A connector seen from the other side is mirrored, and a mirrored connector is the classic mistake: left and right swap, and pin 1 sits at the other end of its row. Check which view you are looking at, and that it shows the mating face of the part you are wiring to. Clone boards can differ from the drawing; the NodeMCU entry says so and asks you to compare with the silk screen before wiring. The TO-92 page lists examples only. The pin order depends on the part and the maker, so check the datasheet of your exact part.

### Debug and interfaces

- ARM JTAG (20-pin)
- Cortex Debug / SWD (10-pin)
- AVR ISP (6-pin)
- FTDI TTL-232R (6-pin)
- Qwiic / STEMMA QT
- Grove (4-pin)
- Hobby servo (3-pin)
- OBD-II (SAE J1962)

### ICs

- NE555 (DIP-8)
- LM317 (TO-220)
- L78xx (TO-220)
- LM358 (DIP-8)
- LM324 (DIP-14)
- SN74HC595 (DIP-16)
- ULN2003A (DIP-16)
- ATmega328P (DIP-28)
- TO-92: examples

## Sources and Honesty

Transcribed standard tables are guide values, cross-checked against two independent sources. Cells that could not be cross-checked are left empty, and a column without any verified value is hidden. Each table names its source; check a design that matters against the standard or the datasheet. Pinouts name their sources the same way, at the foot of each page. Check the pin you wire against the datasheet of your part.

## Using ECalc from the Agent

The AuraGo agent can use ECalc's formulas, reference tables, component codes and pinouts through the `ecalc` tool. The tool computes on your AuraGo server with the same catalog
and formulas as the app. It reads nothing from the network or from files, and it has no switch of its own in **Config**.

The agent has eight operations:

- **search** finds calculators, tables and component codes by a topic, a part or a formula, in English or German. Without a search term it lists the categories.
- **describe** shows the variables of a calculator with their units and defaults, its choices, the sets of inputs that work, the
  values it computes and its checks. For a table it shows the columns and the key; for a component code, the forms it reads and writes; for a pinout, the connector, the view, the pin counts and the variants, but not the pins.
- **calculate** solves a calculator from the values you give. Any complete set of inputs works, so it can solve for whichever value
  is missing. It reports every value in SI units and as formatted text, with the calculator's warnings. It also tells you when a value
  you gave differs from the result by more than 1 %. For a computed resistor it names the nearest standard value of the chosen series,
  and the standard-value combiner returns its pairs.
- **table** reads the rows of a reference table. It filters them, pages through them (`offset`, `limit`) and answers one lookup:
  `exact` (the row whose column equals the value), `ge` (the row with the smallest cell that is at least the value) or `interp` (a value
  between the neighbouring rows). Rows come in the column units, with the SI values for further calculation.
- **pinout** lists the pins of a connector, a board header or an IC package, in pin order. Each pin has its number, name, function,
  type and, where a standard names one, its wire colour. Give `pin` for one pin, by number (`7`) or by name (`GND`; several pins can
  share a name), `variant` for a variant such as `t568b`, or `filter` for a word. The answer also says what the drawing shows (`view`);
  read it before you tell the user where a pin sits.
- **decode** reads a component code, for example the colour bands of a resistor, and reports its value and fields. **encode** writes
  one from a value: it picks the nearest standard value of the series that the tolerance implies and returns the matching marking
  or bands.
- **open** shows a calculator in the ECalc app on the desktop, with the values filled in as if you had typed them. The answer
  computes nothing; for the numbers the agent uses **calculate**. Names and values are checked one by one, but the values are not
  checked against each other, so a set of values that contradict each other opens as typed. For a pinout, **open** opens the pinout's page.

**open** needs the Virtual Desktop to be switched on, and **Allow agent control** to be enabled, in **Config → Integrations →
Virtual Desktop**. Without them the agent gets a "policy denied" answer and gives you the numbers from **calculate** instead.
Other agents that reach AuraGo through A2A (agent-to-agent requests) may use search, describe, calculate, table, pinout, decode and encode, all of which only read, but they cannot open ECalc.

Prompts you can type:

- "What resistor do I need for a red LED at 20 mA on 5 V?" The agent calculates the series resistor with the **LED series resistor**
  calculator and reports the nearest standard value.
- "Open ECalc with the 555 astable for 1 kHz." The agent opens the **NE555 astable (oscillator)** calculator in the Virtual Desktop with
  the frequency filled in, if the Virtual Desktop and agent control are switched on.
- "Which AWG size has a diameter of about 2 mm?" The agent reads the **AWG wire gauges** table with a lookup and names the matching size.
- "What resistor is brown black red gold?" The agent decodes the colour bands with `decode` and reports the value and tolerance.
- "Which pin of a USB-A plug is ground?" The agent reads the pins of **USB 2.0 Type-A** with `pinout` and names pin 4, GND.

## Privacy and Safety

- **On your device.** The calculations in the app run in your browser. ECalc loads its catalog from your AuraGo server and sends none of
  your values anywhere. It loads no external fonts, libraries or services.
- **Agent tool.** The `ecalc` tool computes on your AuraGo server with the catalog built into AuraGo. It reads nothing from the network
  or from files. **open** works only while the Virtual Desktop is switched on and agent control is allowed.
- **Read-only.** ECalc only reads. A read-only Virtual Desktop does not change how it works.
- **Check what matters.** Each calculator names its source under **Explanation**. The results are only as good as the formula
  and your inputs. Check a design that matters against the datasheets of your parts. For a pinout, check the pin against the datasheet of your part before you wire or solder. Mains voltage is dangerous, and ECalc is
  no substitute for qualified electrical work.
- **Mains installations.** The **Cable voltage drop** calculator gives guide values for mains installations. Its page says that the
  design of a mains installation must follow the installation standard (for example DIN VDE 0100-520 or IEC 60364-5-52) and the local
  rules, and that a qualified electrician must carry it out and check it.

## When Something Goes Wrong

| Problem | What helps |
|---------|------------|
| "The ECalc catalog could not be loaded." | Click **Try again**. If it keeps failing, check that AuraGo is running and that you are still signed in, then reload the Virtual Desktop. |
| A field shows a message instead of a value | See the table in [Entering Values](#entering-values). |
| A number-system field shows an error | The digits must match the base: 0 and 1 for binary, 0 to 7 for octal, 0 to 9 and A to F for hexadecimal. The value must stay between 0 and 2^53 − 1 (9 007 199 254 740 991). The prefix of the field's base (`0x`, `0b` or `0o`) is optional. |
| A field is dimmed | The selected option does not use it. For DC in the **Cable voltage drop** calculator, cos φ is dimmed. Choose an option that uses the field if you need it. |
| The agent cannot open ECalc ("policy denied") | Switch on the Virtual Desktop and **Allow agent control** in **Config → Integrations → Virtual Desktop**. Until then the agent can still give you the numbers from **calculate**. |
| The favorites or the last values are gone | They live in the browser. A different browser, a private window or cleared browser data starts with empty ones. |
| The E-series value is far from the calculated one | Choose a series with more values, such as E96 or E192. |
| A table column is hidden | The column has no verified data: its cells could not be cross-checked, so they are left empty and the column is hidden. The line under the table says how many columns are hidden. |
| A finder shows a warning ("Not covered by the verified data") | The inputs lie outside the verified data, or no second source confirmed a value for this combination. Choose another combination; the finder highlights no row. |
| A code is rejected as "not cross-checked" or "ambiguous" | The symbol is not in the verified data ("not cross-checked"), or makers read it in conflicting ways ("ambiguous"). Read the marking on the part and check the datasheet. In the agent tool the answer has the code `unsupported`. |
| The pin table says "No pin matches the filter." | The filter text is not in the number, name, function, type, wire colour or notes of any pin of this variant. Clear the box, or press Escape in it. |
| The **Wire** column is missing | No pin of the variant has a wire colour, because the source gives none. The column appears only when a pin has one. |
`````

`````markdown
# Kapitel 32: ECalc – Elektronik-Formeln im Virtual Desktop

ECalc ist eine Formelsammlung für Elektronik im Virtual Desktop. Eine Rechenseite zeigt die Schaltung, die Formel und die
Ergebnisse nebeneinander und rechnet schon während du tippst. Du gibst die Werte ein, die du kennst, und ECalc berechnet den
Rest. Bei Widerständen schlägt es außerdem den nächsten Normwert aus einer E-Reihe vor, und der Rechner **Kombination von
Normwerten** findet Normwerte, die in Reihe oder parallel einen Zielwiderstand erreichen.

ECalc enthält 79 Rechner in zehn Kategorien, 44 Nachschlagetabellen (siehe [Tabellen](#tabellen)), fünf Bauteilcode-Seiten (siehe
[Bauteilcodes](#bauteilcodes)) und 47 Pinbelegungen von Steckverbindern, Stiftleisten und ICs (siehe [Pinbelegungen](#pinbelegungen)).
Der Agent kann mit denselben Formeln rechnen, Tabellen, Codes und Pinbelegungen lesen und für dich einen
Rechner öffnen (siehe [ECalc mit dem Agenten nutzen](#ecalc-mit-dem-agenten-nutzen)). ECalc läuft in deinem Browser. Es braucht keinen Provider und hat keinen
eigenen Schalter unter **Config**.

## Inhalt
1. [ECalc öffnen](#ecalc-öffnen)
2. [Einen Rechner finden](#einen-rechner-finden)
3. [Die Rechenseite](#die-rechenseite)
4. [Werte eingeben](#werte-eingeben)
5. [Normwerte (E-Reihen)](#normwerte-e-reihen)
6. [Einstellungen](#einstellungen)
7. [Die Rechner](#die-rechner)
8. [Tabellen](#tabellen)
9. [Bauteilcodes](#bauteilcodes)
10. [Pinbelegungen](#pinbelegungen)
11. [Quellen und Grenzen](#quellen-und-grenzen)
12. [ECalc mit dem Agenten nutzen](#ecalc-mit-dem-agenten-nutzen)
13. [Datenschutz und Sicherheit](#datenschutz-und-sicherheit)
14. [Wenn etwas schiefgeht](#wenn-etwas-schiefgeht)

---

## ECalc öffnen

Öffne **ECalc** aus dem Startmenü, in der Kategorie **Entwicklung**. Das Fenster öffnet sich mit etwa 1100 × 760 Pixeln und lässt
sich in der Größe ändern. ECalc öffnet wieder den Rechner, den du zuletzt benutzt hast.

Das Fenster hat drei Spalten: links die **Kategorieleiste**, in der Mitte die **Liste** der Rechner und rechts die
**Rechenseite**. In einem schmalen Fenster (unter etwa 720 Pixeln) wird daraus ein einziger Stapel. Wähle eine Kategorie,
dann einen Rechner, und gehe mit **Zurück** eine Ebene nach oben.

## Einen Rechner finden

- **Kategorieleiste:** Zuerst kommen **Favoriten** und **Zuletzt verwendet**, danach die Kategorien mit Inhalten: Grundlagen, Passive
  Bauteile, Filter, Halbleiter, Stromversorgung, OpAmps, Timer, HF, Digital, Leitungen & PCB, **Tabellen**, **Bauteilcodes** und **Pinbelegungen**.
  Jede Kategorie zeigt, wie viele Einträge sie enthält. Die Leiste zeigt eine Kategorie nur, wenn sie Inhalte hat.
- **Suche:** Tippe oben ins Suchfeld, um einen Rechner, eine Tabelle, einen Bauteilcode oder eine Pinbelegung über seinen Namen in deiner Sprache, über
  den englischen Namen oder über ein Stichwort wie „Teiler“ zu finden. Jeder Eintrag hat Schlagwörter, die die Suche ebenfalls durchsucht.
- **Favoriten:** Die Favoriten-Schaltfläche auf einer Rechenseite nimmt den Rechner in die **Favoriten** auf. Ein weiterer Klick
  entfernt ihn wieder.
- **Zuletzt verwendet:** ECalc merkt sich die letzten 12 Rechner, die du geöffnet hast.

## Die Rechenseite

Eine Rechenseite besteht aus diesen Teilen:

- **Titelzeile:** der Name des Rechners und die Schaltflächen **Zu Favoriten hinzufügen**, **Ergebnisse kopieren** und **Auf
  Standardwerte zurücksetzen**.
- **Schaltplan:** die Schaltung, mit einem Eingabefeld neben jedem Bauteil, zu dem es gehört. Ein Rechner ohne Schaltplan zeigt
  seine Felder in einer einfachen Liste.
- **Formel:** die gesetzte Formel und darunter eine Live-Zeile mit deinen eingesetzten Werten, zum Beispiel
  *V_out = 12 V · 2,2 kΩ / (4,7 kΩ + 2,2 kΩ) = 3,83 V*.
- **Nächste Normwerte:** die E-Reihen-Vorschläge für die Widerstände (siehe [Normwerte (E-Reihen)](#normwerte-e-reihen)).
- **Kombinationen:** nur beim Rechner **Kombination von Normwerten**. Er zeigt den nächsten Einzelwert zum Ziel sowie bis zu fünf
  Paare in Reihe und bis zu fünf Paare parallel, jeweils mit Wert und Abweichung vom Ziel. Der Block trägt die gewählte Reihe als
  Überschrift, zum Beispiel „Kombinationen aus E24-Werten“.
- **Abgeleitete Werte:** weitere Größen, die sich aus dem Ergebnis ergeben, zum Beispiel der Strom durch einen Spannungsteiler
  und seine Leistung.
- **Diagramm:** eine Kurve unter der Formel: ein Wert über einem anderen, von 0 bis zu einem Endwert. Alle übrigen Werte bleiben
  auf den Werten der Seite. Der RC-Zeitkonstanten-Rechner zeichnet zum Beispiel die Kondensatorspannung über die Zeit von 0 bis 5 τ.
  Das Diagramm bleibt ausgeblendet, solange die Werte, die es braucht, unbekannt sind.
- **Warnungen:** ein Hinweis, wenn die Werte keinen Sinn ergeben, zum Beispiel eine Ausgangsspannung, die nicht unter der
  Eingangsspannung liegt.
- **Erklärung:** ein einklappbarer Text zum Rechner mit der **Quelle**: der Norm, dem Datenblatt oder dem Lehrbuch hinter der
  Formel.

**Ergebnisse kopieren** legt die Werte der Seite in die Zwischenablage. **Auf Standardwerte zurücksetzen** stellt die
Startwerte des Rechners wieder her.

**Abgeblendete Felder:** Manche Rechner bieten eine Option, etwa die Stromart eines Kabels (Gleichstrom, einphasiger oder
dreiphasiger Wechselstrom). Ein Feld, das die gewählte Option nicht verwendet, wird abgeblendet, und sein Hinweis lautet „Bei der
gewählten Option nicht verwendet“. Beim Rechner **Spannungsfall im Kabel** ist bei Gleichstrom zum Beispiel cos φ abgeblendet.
Abgeblendete Felder fehlen in **Ergebnisse kopieren** und in den Vorschlägen der E-Reihe.

## Werte eingeben

Jeder Rechner braucht eine feste Anzahl bekannter Werte. Das Ohmsche Gesetz zum Beispiel braucht zwei der vier Größen Spannung,
Strom, Widerstand und Leistung. Die Felder, die du ausfüllst, sind **Eingaben**. ECalc füllt die übrigen Felder mit
**berechneten** Werten und färbt sie ein.

- **Ändern, was bekannt ist:** Tippe in ein berechnetes Feld. Es wird zur Eingabe, und die Eingabe, die du am längsten nicht
  mehr angefasst hast, wird berechnet. So kannst du von dem Wert ausgehen, den du gerade zur Hand hast.
- **Wert sperren:** Das Schlosssymbol an einem Feld hält es fest. Ein gesperrtes Feld bleibt eine Eingabe, bis du es wieder
  entsperrst, auch wenn du andere Felder änderst.
- **Zahlenformate:** Du kannst `4k7` (4,7 kΩ), `2u2` (2,2 µ), `10 mA`, `1e-6` oder `0,5` tippen. Dezimalkomma und Dezimalpunkt
  funktionieren beide. Eine Einheit hinter der Zahl ist optional.
- **Zahlensysteme:** Die vier Felder des Rechners **Zahlensysteme** (dec, hex, bin, oct) zeigen dieselbe ganze Zahl, jedes in
  seiner Basis. Tippe die Zahl in eines der Felder, mit den Ziffern der Basis dieses Feldes. Das Präfix dieser Basis ist optional:
  `0x` für Hexadezimal (`0xFF`), `0b` für Binär (`0b1111_1111`) und `0o` für Oktal (`0o377`). Dezimal nimmt einfache Ziffern
  (`255`), und `_` oder ein Leerzeichen dürfen die Ziffern trennen. Lange Hex- und Binärergebnisse sind zur besseren Lesbarkeit
  gruppiert: Hex zu vier Stellen (`0xDEAD_BEEF`), Binär zu acht (`0b1_00000000`).
- **Einheiten:** Das Auswahlfeld neben einem Feld wählt die Einheit und bietet nur die Einheiten an, die zum Feld passen.
  **Automatisch** wählt ein passendes Präfix, etwa mA oder kΩ. Ein Querschnitt bietet mm², AWG und kcmil, eine Temperatur °C, °F
  und K, und die Kupferdicke einer Leiterbahn oz (Kupfergewicht). Manche Felder bieten besondere Einheiten, etwa dBm, dBV und dBu
  für Pegel oder mAh, Ah und Wh für Ladung und Energie.
- **Listen:** Der Rechner für Reihen- und Parallelschaltung nimmt eine Liste wie `4k7, 10k, 2k2`. Trenne die Einträge mit
  Kommas, Semikolons oder Leerzeichen. Ein Komma direkt vor einer Ziffer ist ein Dezimalkomma: `4,7k, 10k` sind zwei Einträge
  (4,7 kΩ und 10 kΩ), `1,2,3` dagegen ein Eintrag, der sich nicht lesen lässt. Setze nach einem Komma zwischen Einträgen ein
  Leerzeichen.
- **Anzeige:** Die Ergebnisse zeigen in Deutsch, Tschechisch, Dänisch, Griechisch, Spanisch, Französisch, Italienisch,
  Niederländisch, Norwegisch, Polnisch, Portugiesisch und Schwedisch ein Dezimalkomma, in den anderen Sprachen einen
  Dezimalpunkt. Listen zeigen immer einen Dezimalpunkt, weil das Komma ihre Einträge trennt.

Wenn etwas nicht stimmt, zeigt das Feld eine Meldung statt einer Zahl:

| Meldung | Bedeutung |
|---------|-----------|
| „Gib weitere Werte ein, um das zu berechnen.“ | Die bekannten Werte bestimmen dieses Feld noch nicht. |
| „Mit diesen Werten gibt es kein endliches Ergebnis.“ | Die Rechnung teilt durch null oder verlässt den Zahlenbereich. |
| „Dieser Wert muss größer als null sein.“ | Ein Widerstand zum Beispiel kann nicht null oder negativ sein. |
| „Dieser Wert ist nicht lesbar. Beispiele: 4k7, 10 mA, 1e-6.“ | Der Text ist keine Zahl mit optionalem Präfix und optionaler Einheit. Deine bisherigen Werte bleiben unverändert. |

## Normwerte (E-Reihen)

Widerstände gibt es in Normwerten. Jedes Widerstandsfeld eines Rechners zeigt **Nächster E24-Wert**: den nächstliegenden Normwert
und wie weit er vom berechneten Wert abweicht, in Prozent. 4,7 kΩ zum Beispiel gehört zur E24-Reihe, und ein berechneter Wert von
4,6 kΩ würde 4,7 kΩ mit einer Abweichung von etwa +2,2 % zeigen.

Eine andere Reihe (E6 bis E192) wählst du im Auswahlfeld **E-Reihe**. Voreingestellt ist E24. Reihen mit mehr Werten, etwa E96,
ergeben eine kleinere Abweichung. ECalc merkt sich deine Wahl.

**Kombination von Normwerten.** Der Rechner **Kombination von Normwerten** in den Grundlagen macht aus einem Zielwiderstand
Normwerte. Er nutzt dasselbe Auswahlfeld **E-Reihe**. Er zeigt den nächsten Einzelwert der gewählten Reihe sowie bis zu fünf Paare
in Reihe und bis zu fünf Paare parallel. Jedes Paar zeigt seinen Gesamtwert und seine Abweichung vom Ziel in Prozent. Beispiel: 5 kΩ
aus der E12-Reihe ergeben 4,7 kΩ + 270 Ω (−0,6 %) oder 10 kΩ parallel zu 10 kΩ (genau 5 kΩ).

## Einstellungen

Das Einstellungsmenü hat zwei Optionen:

- **Signifikante Stellen:** wie viele Stellen die Ergebnisse zeigen, von 3 bis 6. Voreingestellt sind 4.
- **Schaltsymbole:** **IEC** zeichnet den Widerstand als Rechteck (Voreinstellung). **ANSI** zeichnet den Zickzack-Widerstand.

ECalc speichert seine Einstellungen, deine Favoriten, die Liste der zuletzt verwendeten Rechner, die gewählten Einheiten und die
letzten Werte jedes Rechners im Browser unter dem Schlüssel `aurago.ecalc.v1`. Sie bleiben in diesem Browser. Auf dem
AuraGo-Server wird nichts gespeichert, und wer die Browserdaten löscht, setzt sie zurück. ECalc funktioniert auch ohne
Browser-Speicher, vergisst dann aber alles, sobald du das Fenster schließt.

## Die Rechner

ECalc enthält 79 Rechner in zehn Kategorien. Jede Tabelle listet die Rechner einer Kategorie, in der Reihenfolge der
Kategorieleiste. Die Quelle hinter jeder Formel, also die Norm, das Datenblatt oder das Lehrbuch, zeigt die Seite des Rechners
unter **Erklärung**; deshalb steht sie nicht in den Tabellen.

### Grundlagen

| Rechner | Was er macht |
|---------|--------------|
| Ohmsches Gesetz und Leistung | Spannung, Strom, Widerstand und Leistung. Gib zwei beliebige Größen ein und erhalte die beiden anderen. |
| Spannungsteiler | Die Ausgangsspannung eines Teilers aus zwei Widerständen. Er findet auch einen Widerstand oder die Eingangsspannung für eine gewünschte Ausgangsspannung und zeigt Strom und Leistung. |
| Belasteter Spannungsteiler | Derselbe Teiler mit einem Lastwiderstand am Ausgang. Er zeigt zum Vergleich die unbelastete Ausgangsspannung und warnt, wenn die Last das Ziel unmöglich macht. |
| Stromteiler | Wie sich ein Strom auf zwei parallele Widerstände verteilt. |
| Reihen- und Parallelschaltung | Der Gesamtwiderstand einer Liste von Widerständen, in Reihe und parallel. |
| Dezibel-Verhältnis | Rechnet zwischen einem Verhältnis und Dezibel um. Wähle Spannung (20 log) oder Leistung (10 log). |
| Pegel in dB | Spannung, Widerstand und Leistung mit den Pegeln in dBm, dBV und dBu. |
| Wheatstone-Brücke | Die Brückenspannung aus der Versorgung und vier Widerständen, oder der Widerstand, der die Brücke abgleicht. |
| Stern-Dreieck-Umwandlung | Wandelt drei Dreieck-Widerstände in den gleichwertigen Stern um und umgekehrt. |
| Effektiv-, Spitzen- und Mittelwert | Rechnet zwischen Effektivwert, Spitzenwert, Spitze-Spitze-Wert und Mittelwert einer Sinus-, Rechteck- oder Dreieckschwingung um. |
| Ladung und Energie | Rechnet zwischen Ladung (zum Beispiel den mAh eines Akkus), Spannung und Energie (Wh oder J) um. |
| Kombination von Normwerten | Der nächste Normwert zu einem Zielwiderstand sowie Paare in Reihe oder parallel, die am nächsten kommen. |

### Passive Bauteile

| Rechner | Was er macht |
|---------|--------------|
| Kapazitiver Blindwiderstand | Blindwiderstand eines Kondensators. Je zwei der Größen Frequenz, Kapazität und Blindwiderstand ergeben die dritte. |
| Induktiver Blindwiderstand | Blindwiderstand einer Spule. Je zwei der Größen Frequenz, Induktivität und Blindwiderstand ergeben die dritte. |
| Impedanz der Reihenschaltung (RC, RL, RLC) | Resultierender Blindwiderstand, Impedanz und Phasenwinkel eines Widerstands in Reihe mit Spule, Kondensator oder beidem. |
| Impedanz der Parallelschaltung (RC, RL, RLC) | Impedanzbetrag, Phasenwinkel und äquivalenter Parallelblindwiderstand eines Widerstands parallel zu Spule, Kondensator oder beidem. |
| RC-Zeitkonstante | Auf- und Entladen eines Kondensators über einen Widerstand, mit der Zeitkonstante und dem Spannungsverlauf. |
| Reihen- und Parallelschaltung von Kondensatoren | Gesamtkapazität einer Liste von Kondensatoren, in Reihe und parallel. |
| Reihen- und Parallelschaltung von Spulen | Gesamtinduktivität einer Liste von Spulen, in Reihe und parallel, ohne magnetische Kopplung. |
| Kondensatorenergie und -ladung | Energie, Ladung, Spannung und Kapazität eines Kondensators. Je zwei davon ergeben die beiden anderen. |
| Luftspule (Wheeler) | Induktivität einer einlagigen Luftspule aus Durchmesser, Länge und Windungszahl, oder eine dieser Größen für eine gewünschte Induktivität. |
| Ringkerninduktivität (A_L) | Induktivität eines Ringkerns aus seinem A_L-Wert und der Windungszahl, oder eine der drei Größen. |
| Leitungswiderstand | Gleichstromwiderstand eines Kupfer-, Aluminium- oder Silberleiters, mit Temperaturkorrektur. Löst auch nach Länge, Querschnitt oder Temperatur auf. |

### Filter

| Rechner | Was er macht |
|---------|--------------|
| RC-Tiefpass | Grenzfrequenz und Verhalten eines Tiefpasses erster Ordnung bei einer Testfrequenz. |
| RC-Hochpass | Grenzfrequenz und Verhalten eines Hochpasses erster Ordnung bei einer Testfrequenz. |
| LC-Schwingkreis | Resonanzfrequenz eines LC-Kreises und sein Kennwiderstand. |
| RLC-Kreis: Güte und Bandbreite | Güte und −3-dB-Bandbreite eines Reihen- oder Parallel-RLC-Kreises. |
| Sallen-Key-Tiefpass (Verstärkung 1) | Aktiver Tiefpass zweiter Ordnung mit gleichen Widerständen und den Kondensatorwerten für einen Butterworth-Verlauf. |
| Doppel-T-Sperrfilter | Sperrfrequenz des passiven Doppel-T-Netzwerks. |
| Pi-Dämpfungsglied | Widerstände eines angepassten π-Glieds für eine Systemimpedanz und eine Dämpfung in dB. |
| T-Dämpfungsglied | Widerstände eines angepassten T-Glieds für eine Systemimpedanz und eine Dämpfung in dB. |

### Halbleiter

| Rechner | Was er macht |
|---------|--------------|
`````
